name: Grape diet (grape therapy)

lead: The grape diet, also called grape therapy, grape cure or ampelotherapy, is a regimen built around eating fresh grapes, in its strict form to the exclusion of other foods for days or weeks. Followers describe it as cleansing and credit the fruit's polyphenols and water content for fresher-looking skin and a lighter feel.

It dates to 19th-century German spa practice and was popularised by Johanna Brandt's book The Grape Cure in the 1920s. Modern research looks at grape or grape-powder intake and markers such as blood clotting and inflammation, mostly in animals; the exclusive-grape regimen itself has not been studied in trials.

paras: The traditional form replaces meals with grapes, including skins and seeds, for a set period before returning to normal food. Milder modern versions simply add grapes or grape products to meals. People sometimes combine it with fasting-style approaches.

Dietitian sources say fruit-only eating lacks adequate protein, B12, calcium, iron and other nutrients, and raises sugar and dental concerns. It is described as unsuitable for children, teens and pregnancy. Brandt's cancer-cure claim is regarded by critics as quackery.

chain: Eat grapes, rich in polyphenols and water
Proponents say this cleanses and reduces inflammation
angle.text: Followers use grape days or a grape-focused plan hoping for a clearer, fresher complexion and reduced bloating. The link to appearance is a claim by proponents; the research on grapes concerns other outcomes.

lead: The grape diet, known historically as the grape cure or ampelotherapy, is a health regimen centred on eating fresh grapes, traditionally as the main or only food for a period. Proponents describe it as detoxifying and skin-clearing; for looksmaxxing, it is discussed as a way to cleanse and brighten the complexion.[1]

Accounts date the modern practice to German spa towns in the mid-19th century, with physician Veit Kaufmann promoting an exclusive grape diet, and to South African writer Johanna Brandt, whose book The Grape Cure (published in the 1920s) described her own claimed recovery from stomach cancer.[1][2] Critic Stephen Barrett of Quackwatch has labelled its conclusions quackery.[2]

Research on grapes themselves is separate from the diet. A controlled trial of 30 healthy volunteers, 20 of whom ate grapes daily for three weeks, found reduced thrombin generation and more fibrinolysis-susceptible clots.[3] Other work is in mice and rats.[1] Nutrition sources describe fruit-only diets as lacking several nutrients.[4]

paras: Grape therapy centres on whole grapes, including skins and sometimes seeds, with proponents claiming detoxification, alkalising and anti-inflammatory effects from polyphenols such as resveratrol and anthocyanins.[1] A softer modern form simply increases grape intake.

Practices using grapes in spa treatments appear in 19th-century Europe, notably in Bad Dürkheim, Germany, and later in France (cure uvale) at stations such as Moissac.[1] Johanna Brandt (1876-1964), a South African writer and activist, published The Grape Cure and wrote that she had cured her own stomach cancer; its influence reached later authors, and her claims are unverified in independent sources.[2]

Health sources on fruit-only diets state that they can lead to shortfalls in protein, calcium, iron, zinc, vitamin D, B12 and essential fatty acids, and that restrictive eating may trigger orthorexia. They are described as unsuitable for children, teens and pregnancy.[4]

A controlled clinical trial in 30 healthy volunteers (20 eating grapes at 5 g per kg of body weight daily for three weeks, 10 controls) reported decreases in procoagulant activity and thrombin generation that persisted after a four-week wash-out, with clots more susceptible to fibrinolysis.[3] That study did not examine appearance or a grape-only regimen. Other grape studies cited in the literature are in rodents.[1]

timeline.event: Veit Kaufmann publishes on an exclusive grape diet in Germany, according to Grokipedia.[1]
Johanna Brandt publishes The Grape Cure.[2]
Quackwatch critic Stephen Barrett labels its conclusions quackery.[2]
Controlled trial of grape intake and coagulation published.[3]
